segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The book of the origin of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Abraham fathered Isaac, Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, Perez fathered Hezron, and Hezron fathered Ram.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, and Nahshon fathered Salmon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, and Obed fathered Jesse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesse fathered David the king. David fathered Solomon by Uriah’s wife.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Solomon fathered Rehoboam, Rehoboam fathered Abijah, and Abijah fathered Asaph.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Asaph fathered Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat fathered Joram, and Joram fathered Uzziah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Uzziah fathered Jotham, Jotham fathered Ahaz, and Ahaz fathered Hezekiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Hezekiah fathered Manasseh, Manasseh fathered Amos, and Amos fathered Josiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Josiah fathered Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel, and Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Zerubbabel fathered Abiud, Abiud fathered Eliakim, and Eliakim fathered Azor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Azor fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Achim, and Achim fathered Eliud.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Eliud fathered Eleazar, Eleazar fathered Matthan, and Matthan fathered Jacob.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Messiah fourteen generations.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the origin of Jesus Christ was like this. His mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, but before they came together she was found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Joseph her husband, being a righteous man and not wanting to expose her to public disgrace, decided to divorce her quietly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when he had thought this over, look, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take home Mary your wife, for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: She will give birth to a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All this took place to fulfill what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Look, the virgin will become pregnant and give birth to a son, and they will name him Emmanuel,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which is translated “God with us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and took his wife home,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but he did not have sexual relations with her until she had given birth to a son, and he named him Jesus.

notes.traditional: The book of the genealogy (or “generation”) of Jesus Christ
notes.note: The Greek word is the one that gives the first book of the Bible its name, and the phrase echoes the Greek of Genesis 2:4 and 5:1. Most translations render it “genealogy” here and “birth” in verse 18. “Origin” is used in both places so that the reader can see Matthew using the same word twice. Whether the heading covers the genealogy only, the opening chapters or the whole book is disputed.

Jewish genealogies normally ran through fathers only. Matthew names four mothers before Mary—Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and “Uriah’s wife” (Bathsheba)—passing over the famous matriarchs. Why he chose these four is debated; common suggestions are that they were foreigners or linked to foreigners, or that each became a mother in the royal line in irregular circumstances, preparing the reader for Mary.

The earliest manuscripts read “Asaph” here and “Amos” in verse 10, where the Old Testament kings are Asa and Amon; later manuscripts have the expected names. Many English versions print “Asa” and “Amon”. This translation follows the Greek text as edited. Whether Matthew used variant spellings of the kings’ names or intended an allusion to the psalmist and the prophet is uncertain.

The Greek word translates the Hebrew “Messiah”, the anointed king Israel expected. Where it functions as a title, as here and in verse 17, this translation uses “Messiah”; where it is attached to “Jesus” as part of his name (verses 1 and 18), it uses “Christ”. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

After thirty-nine repetitions of “fathered”, the pattern breaks: Joseph is not said to have fathered Jesus. The verb turns passive, and “of whom” is feminine singular in Greek, referring to Mary alone. The rest of the chapter explains the break.

The list is shaped to give three groups of fourteen; for example, three kings known from the Old Testament are passed over between Joram and Uzziah, and the third group has fourteen names only if Jeconiah is counted again. A widely held suggestion is that fourteen is the sum of the Hebrew letters of the name David, but Matthew does not say so and the explanation is not certain.

Jewish betrothal was a binding legal contract, much more than a modern engagement. The couple were already called husband and wife (verses 19–20), unfaithfulness counted as adultery, and the bond could be ended only by divorce. The marriage was completed, often about a year later, when the husband took the bride into his home, which is what “take home” refers to in verses 20 and 24.

Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice); here the word describes a man who keeps God’s law. The connection with what follows can be read two ways: because he was righteous he could not go through with the marriage but chose the kindest way out, or although he was righteous he did not want to shame her. The translation leaves both open.

“Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yeshua, a shortened form of Joshua, which was understood to mean “the Lord saves”. The angel’s explanation, “for he will save his people”, plays on that meaning. The wordplay works in Hebrew or Aramaic and is not visible in Greek or English.

Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14 in its Greek form, where the word normally means a virgin. The Hebrew of Isaiah has a word meaning a young woman of marriageable age, which does not in itself specify virginity. Isaiah has “you will call” or “she will call” where Matthew has “they will name”.

notes.phrase: did not have sexual relations with her until
notes.note: The Greek says literally that he “did not know her”, a biblical idiom for sexual intercourse. “Until” fixes what was true up to the birth and does not by itself say what happened afterward. Most Protestant interpreters take it to imply normal marital relations later, while Catholic and Orthodox tradition holds that Mary remained a virgin; the Greek does not settle it. Some later manuscripts read “her firstborn son”, probably taken from Luke 2:7.

candidates.rendering: fathered (active, of a father); was born (passive); conceived (passive, of the unborn child)
candidates.reason: The verb covers begetting, bearing and being born across the Gospels, John and 1 John (“born of God”), and the English needs to be controlled so that readers can follow the connections.
The word is extremely frequent in narrative and speech, and translators vary between “behold”, “look”, “see”, “suddenly” and leaving it out, so one policy is needed.
It recurs in Luke 1–2, and the choice between “betrothed”, “engaged” and “pledged to be married” affects how readers understand the legal status of Mary and Joseph.
In the marital sense it recurs in the divorce sayings (Matthew 5 and 19, Mark 10, Luke 16) and should be kept distinct from its other senses of “release” and “send away”.
Matthew’s fulfillment formula recurs about ten times and the verb is used of Scripture across the New Testament, so the rendering of formula and verb should be fixed.
